definition: In this context, a sleeper effect is a delayed outcome in which an early experience or deprivation does not show its full impact until much later in development. It refers to a later-emerging change in how emotional information is mentally represented, suggesting that early visual input helps shape abilities that continue to develop after birth.

reasons: The packet supports a postnatal refinement timeline (“continues to be refined until late childhood”) and that adult cataract-reversal patients show altered emotion representations, but it does not explicitly define a general “sleeper effect” as “an early experience…does not show its full impact until much later in development.” The definition’s generalized criterion (“does not show its full impact until much later”) is not directly stated in the packet.

The definition includes “early visual input helps shape abilities that continue to develop after birth.” The packet supports early visual experience shaping later development of emotion representations and that the emotion structure emerges postnatally, but it specifically refers to shaping representations of emotions rather than “abilities” broadly; this wording is broader than what the packet evidences.
